title: The Problem
description: Climate issues and climate literacy resources from Bay Area Youth Conservation.

thesis.heading: Misbeliefs prevent forward motion in crafting viable solutions to climate change
thesis.lede: Climate literacy and action matter more now than ever. False information and misconceptions ultimately hinder our progress toward a sustainable future. How can we tackle issues that we do not fully understand?
thesis.body: The vast majority of the world agrees that something must be done to reduce global warming. 62% of Americans feel a personal duty to reduce the effects of climate change. However, global emissions has increased, with human-produced greenhouse gases rising 49% since 1990.

blockOne.heading: California's temperatures is rising due to increasing emissions of greenhouse gases
blockOne.body: According to the California Environmental Protection Agency, weather extremes are intensifying and has become more erratic. The increase in greenhouse gas emissions has led average air temperatures to increase by about 2.5 degrees F since 1895. As a result, a multitude of problems has arose. Hotter and drier conditions has led to the increase of reports of work-related heat illnesses tripling in the past 20 years along with the raise of deadly wildfires and wildfire smoke and a significant loss of California's glaciers.

blockTwo.heading: How does this impact the Bay Area?
blockTwo.body: Carbon dioxide is produced as a byproduct of burning fossil fuels. In the Bay Area, roughly 33% of carbon footprints are from transportation and motor vehicles, including 9.7 metric tons from fuels and .5 metric tons from motor vehicle manufacturing and repairs. Carbon emission rates raising leads to a warmer climate because it traps heat in the atmosphere. A warmer climate causes thermal expansion in water and increased volumes of land-ice being moved to the oceans.

findings: "One inundation scenario for the Bay Area according to new data from a USGS report on sea level rise in California. The scenario pictured reflects a rise of 3.3 feet, which is within the projected range according to the 4th California Climate Assessment of 2016."

Without any additional protections in place, 3 ft (0.91 m) of sea level rise could pose serious flood risks in vulnerable areas in and around the city/county (but not limited to) of Marin county, San Leandro, San Francisco, Oakland International Airport, and parts of Corte Madera and San Rafael.
By 2050, almost $18 billion worth of residential and commercial buildings could be flooded due to sea level rise

And according to the 2017 San Leandro Climate Hazard Assessment, the city is at a high risk of sea-level rise. Neighborhoods and infrastructure along the shoreline are particularly vulnerable, including wastewater treatment plants.
